details:
**Sicilian Expedition**
The disastrous Athenian campaign of 415–413 BC during the Peloponnesian War, aimed at capturing Syracuse, Sicily's leading Greek city. It ended with the near-total destruction of the Athenian force and is the single most common clue for the island.

**Alcibiades and the mutilation of the Hermai**
Alcibiades was the chief planner and champion of the Sicilian Expedition. Just before the fleet sailed, the herms (Hermai) statues across Athens were vandalized and the blame fell partly on him; he was recalled from Sicily to stand trial and instead defected to Sparta.

**Nicias and the lunar eclipse**
Nicias opposed the expedition but was made one of its commanders. When a lunar eclipse occurred in 413 BC as the Athenians prepared to withdraw, he insisted on waiting 27 days on the advice of seers, letting the Syracusans trap the army. He was executed after the surrender.

**Gylippus and Lamachus**
Gylippus was the Spartan general sent to organize the defense of Syracuse, turning the tide against Athens. Lamachus was the third, aggressive Athenian commander, killed during the fighting around the Syracusan siege walls.

**Archimedes' heat ray and claw**
The inventor Archimedes of Syracuse defended his city against the Roman siege under Marcus Claudius Marcellus (214–212 BC) during the Second Punic War. Legend credits him with a heat ray of mirrors that set ships on fire, and he built the "Claw of Archimedes," a crane-like device that lifted enemy ships out of the water.

**"Do not disturb my circles"**
Archimedes' legendary last words to the Roman soldier who killed him while he was drawing geometric figures in the sand, after Syracuse fell to Marcellus during a festival to Artemis.

**Sicilian Vespers**
A 1282 revolt that began at the hour of Vespers on Easter Monday outside a church in Palermo, in which Sicilians massacred the French officials of Charles of Anjou. Peter III of Aragon then claimed the island, setting off the War of the Sicilian Vespers. Rioters supposedly identified Frenchmen by asking them to pronounce the Sicilian word for "chickpeas" (ciciri).

**Peace of Caltabellotta**
The 1302 treaty that ended the War of the Sicilian Vespers, leaving Sicily under an Aragonese prince (Frederick III) while the Angevins kept Naples. The earlier Treaty of Anagni (1295) had attempted to settle the same dispute.

**Mamertines and the First Punic War**
The Mamertines were Campanian mercenaries, originally hired by Agathocles of Syracuse, who seized the city of Messana. Threatened by Hiero II of Syracuse, they appealed to Rome, sparking the First Punic War (264–241 BC), most of which was fought on Sicily; Rome gained the island at the war's end.

**Robert Guiscard and the Norman conquest**
Robert Guiscard ("the Cunning" or "the Fox") and his brother Roger I (Roger Bosso), sons of Tancred of Hauteville, conquered Muslim Sicily in the 11th century, winning battles like Misilmeri. Anna Komnene described Robert, who fought her father Alexios at Dyrrhachium and was the father of Bohemond, as "in mind most cunning."

**Roger II and the Tabula Rogeriana**
Roger II founded the Norman Kingdom of Sicily in 1130. He commissioned the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi to produce the Tabula Rogeriana (1154), a world map oriented with south at the top. His son William I ("the Bad") fought his chancellor Maio of Bari.

**Expedition of the Thousand**
Giuseppe Garibaldi's 1860 campaign in which about a thousand volunteer "Redshirts" landed at Marsala, won battles like Calatafimi and Milazzo, and overthrew the Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (Sicily plus Naples) under Francis II, a key step in Italian unification.

**Operation Husky**
The Allied invasion of Sicily in July 1943 during World War II, approved at the Trident Conference. It was preceded by the British deception Operation Mincemeat, and its launch helped push Hitler to call off the Kursk offensive; it opened the way to the invasion of mainland Italy.

**Battle of Himera**
The 480 BC battle in which Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas (Agrigentum) defeated a large Carthaginian invasion of Sicily, traditionally said to have happened on the same day as the Battle of Salamis.

**Syracusan tyrants and Phalaris**
Syracuse was ruled by tyrants including Gelon, Hiero I and II, and Dionysius I and II; the historian Philistus wrote about the Dionysii, whose court hosted Plato and the poet Philoxenus. Phalaris, tyrant of Acragas, was said to roast victims in a hollow brazen bull and was supposedly burned in it himself.

**Aghlabid conquest and Emirate of Sicily**
In 827 the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya invaded Sicily, aided by a rebellion against Byzantine emperor Michael II; the fall of Taormina in 902 completed the Muslim conquest. The Fatimids later replaced the Aghlabids, and the island became the Emirate of Sicily until the Norman conquest.

**Sextus Pompey and the Servile Wars**
Sextus Pompey, son of Pompey the Great, used Sicily as a base to blockade Italy until his defeat in 36 BC. Earlier, Sicily was the site of the First and Second Servile Wars, large slave revolts against Rome in the late 2nd century BC.
